title: Is your outbound about you or your customer?
metaTitle: Who your outbound copy is about
description: Buyers are only thinking about their own problems. Read your last three email campaigns or social posts and check who they're about.
dek: Buyers scroll past copy that isn't about their problems. Read your last three campaigns line by line and count the lines about you.
author: Shane Kennedy

video.title: Who your outbound is about. Marketing for IT firms

images.alt: “Is your outbound about you?” in bold capitals, beside a man thinking with a phone to his chin

shortVersion: Outbound copy is often about the firm sending it: the company, its services, its features and benefits.
Buyers are only thinking about their problems. If they can't see their problem answered in what you've written, they scroll past.
Go back through your last three campaigns and count the lines about you. If that's most of them, there's work to do.

beats.heading: Who the copy is about
body: Take a look at your last three email campaigns or social posts. Are they about your customer, or are they about you?
The best outbound campaigns cover emails, sequences and social posts. But a lot of the copy or messaging is often about you: your company, your services, your features and benefits.
When you know a service inside out, it's the first thing you reach for when you sit down to write.

right.title: About your customer
rows: The outcomes you help them achieve

beats.heading: The Monday morning inbox
body: Buyers are only thinking about their problems. If they can't see an answer to that in what you're saying, they'll scroll past it.
Picture an IT manager clearing their inbox on a Monday morning, with a few tickets already open and a meeting at nine, and they'll stop for anything that sounds like the week they're having.

graphic.eyebrow: How an email about you gets read

steps.text: An email about your company and services
The buyer reads it for their own problems
Can't see their problem in it

beats.heading: Test your last three campaigns
body: Go back through your recent email campaigns and social posts. See whether most of the content is talking about you or talking about your customer.
Do it line by line. Mark each sentence "us" or "them". A line about your certifications is "us". A line about tickets piling up while the team is short-staffed is "them".

graphic.prompt: Tick each campaign that's mostly about the customer.
graphic.privacyNote: Nothing you tick is stored or sent.

beats.heading: If it's mostly about you
body: If it's mostly about your business, you've got some work to do.

The rework doesn't mean starting again. Keep what you offer, and lead with the problem it fixes. "Our service desk never closes" becomes something closer to "Tickets raised overnight get picked up overnight".

graphic.sticker: Tickets raised overnight get picked up overnight
graphic.caption: Illustration, made-up lines

take.line: The rule of thumb is to always write about your customer's reality
take.key: and the outcomes you help them achieve.
body: Once you've reworked a campaign, run the same count on the new version before it goes out.
Outbound is part of Centurion, the strategy we run with IT firms.

notes: The service desk lines are illustrations, not a real firm's copy.
